questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z=2\sqrt{5}x+2y$ that is bounded by the constraints $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2\sqrt{5}x+2y,\,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\sqrt{5}x+2y)=2\sqrt{5}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{5}x+2y)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(2\sqrt{5})}^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+20+4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{25}\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =5\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =5\cdot (1-(-1))\cdot (2-0) \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of $z=3{x}^{2}-y$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=3{x}^{2}-y,\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-y)=6x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-y)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(6x)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+36{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+36{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\sqrt{2+36{x}^{2}}.$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=2y+{x}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=8x,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2y+{x}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 8x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/d2ca6ee66367bd86cd56fe3a4891dbd4b64d9e23d5b4d97c9650b3af184b423f.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+{x}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+{x}^{2})=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{8x}\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8x\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=5+4{x}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8x\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 1 \\ u & 5 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}8x\sqrt{5+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{5}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{5}^{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({9}^{3/2}-{5}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(27-5\sqrt{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\sqrt{1+4x}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{1+4x}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/9a459a9807befc312528771626dca293a7ebbccd97a2c1e938f47a2d90a36726.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3})=2\sqrt{x}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(2\sqrt{x})}^{2}+(0)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1+4x}}\sqrt{1+4x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+4x}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{1+4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+4x}\cdot \sqrt{1+4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(1+4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x+2{x}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(2+8)-0 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the cone $y=4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$ that lies inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le \frac{1}{4}.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}})=\frac{4x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}})=\frac{4z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{4x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(\frac{4z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{16{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}+\frac{16{z}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{17({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{17}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{17}\,$ and $\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le \frac{1}{4}.$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $x=\frac{y-z}{3}$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by the constraints $1\le y\le 4$ and $1\le z\le 3.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x=\frac{y-z}{3},\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 4,\,1\le z\le 3},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/3f06a9c686a935cb6c561affbcd224045618d9cacaf94eb7c9eab8a9ca8da44c.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y-z}{3})=\frac{1}{3}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{y-z}{3})=-\frac{1}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{9}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{11}{9}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{3}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{3}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{3}\cdot (4-1)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =2\sqrt{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z=xy$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=xy,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/f0faa92e0f89c86248abffad7f61cac5d94a3848a7f7be4464c4b28d3915aa32.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)=x,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(y)^{2}+(x)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi \cdot {[\frac{2}{3}\,{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}[{2}^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{2\pi (2\sqrt{2}-1)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $y=3x+2z$ that is subject to the constraints ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 16,\,x\le 0$ and $z\ge 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=3x+2z,\,(x,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 16,\,x\le 0,\,z\ge 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/48ffe2b0bd40937205d9b9d3b6cc264f83bd56ea30a5df318ba7c7507efb68f7.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x+2z)=3, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(3x+2z)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(3)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9+4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{14}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{14}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{14}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{4}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot [\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 8 \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z = y - 4x$ that is bounded by the constraints $0 \leq x \leq 2$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z = f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = y - 4x, \qquad 0 \leq x \leq 2, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4x)=-4, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4x)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-4)^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+16+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{18}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\cdot (2-0)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the plane $z = 2y+2x$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\cos{x}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = 2y+2x, \qquad (x,y)\in D,
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq y \leq \cos{x} \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/e74d609a1288446f0f3adc0de65b814f2a6daaf2d398478e7834882f3be68c8c.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+2x)=2, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+2x)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =3(1-0) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

                    Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as X=F(Y,Z) or Y=F(X,Z)
canonical_examples.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $x =y+\sqrt 2 z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by the constraints $1 \leq y\leq 2$ and $1 \leq z \leq 3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x = y+\sqrt 2 z, \qquad (y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 2, \: 1 \leq z \leq 3\big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/240ac546b0dd725e392dd0bd475b2ef00eebce2594be5921285e227137538c46.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=1, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(1)}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (2-1)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Changing to Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the cone $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ that is subject to the constraints  $x^2 + y^2 \leq 4,\, x\geq 0$ and $y\geq 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\in D,
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x^2+y^2\leq 4, \, x\geq 0, \, y\geq 0 \big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/be8246dc3bfe1bf16af5d9913fc4e6aef58ddad282646a00d3e31120f6bf31e8.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

Now, if our surface $S$ is defined as $z= f(x,y),$ then it can always be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf r(x,y)= \left\langle x,\: y,\: f(x,y)\right\rangle  \qquad (x,y)  \in D.
$$

In this case, the variables $x$ and $y$ act as parameters. 

Thus, the fundamental vector product of $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂f}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨-\frac{∂f}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂f}{∂y},\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and using the fact that $z = f(x,y),$ we can write this as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨-\frac{∂z}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂z}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| = \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}.
$$

So, we conclude that for a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Let's look at an example of how to apply this formula.

tutorials.name: A Worked Example
tutorials.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119930/assets/867722106ffd8445b62a98ab43197ac2fba646faff95017ef7e92c254a97fb6e.png)

  

The surface $S$ shown above consists of the part of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ that lies under the plane $z=9.$ Let's compute the surface area of $S.$

The plane intersects the paraboloid when $z=9.$ Thus, the curve that describes the intersection points is

$$
x^2+y^2 = 9,
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Therefore, our surface can be described by the equations

$$
z = f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2, \quad (x,y) \in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{(x,y): \, x^2 + y^2 \le 9\right\}.
$$

To compute the surface area of $S,$ we use the formula

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our surface area formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by changing the variables to polar coordinates $(x,y)\to (r,\theta),$ we have $\textrm dA = r\,\textrm d r\, \textrm d \theta.$ Thus, our integration region becomes

$$
\Delta = \left\{(r,\theta): \, 0\leq r\leq 3,\:0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+4(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,d\theta \,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{1}{12}{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(37\sqrt{37}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the area of our surface is 

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S =  \dfrac{\pi}{6}(37\sqrt{37} -1).
$$

tutorials.name: Cases Where the Domain Is the XZ- or YZ-Plane
tutorials.problem:
We have similar formulas for the areas of surfaces defined by $x = f(y,z)$ and $y = f(x,z){:}$

- For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $yz$-plane.

- For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $xz$-plane.

Let's see some examples.
